claim: Dysregulated gene expression contributes to most prevalent features in human cancers.
source: Dysregulated gene expression contributes to most prevalent features in human cancers.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about cancer biology.

claim: Most subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) depend on the aberrant assembly of MYB transcriptional co-activator complex.
source: Here, we show that most subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) depend on the aberrant assembly of MYB transcriptional co-activator complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including cell viability assays across multiple AML subtypes and mechanistic studies.

claim: Peptidomimetic interference with the binding of CBP/P300 to MYB does not affect CREB or MLL1 binding.
source: By rapid and selective peptidomimetic interference with the binding of CBP/P300 to MYB, but not CREB or MLL1, we find that the leukemic functions of MYB are mediated by CBP/P300 co-activation of a distinct set of transcription factor complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing selective disruption of MYB:CBP/P300 but not CREB:CBP/P300 interactions (Figure 3B).

claim: MYB complexes assemble aberrantly with LYL1, E2A, C/EBP family members, LMO2, and SATB1 in AML cells.
source: These MYB complexes assemble aberrantly with LYL1, E2A, C/EBP family members, LMO2, and SATB1.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and mass spectrometry data identifying these factors in MYB complexes (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Aberrant MYB complexes are organized convergently in genetically diverse subtypes of AML.
source: They are organized convergently in genetically diverse subtypes of AML and are at least in part associated with inappropriate transcription factor co-expression.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments across seven genetically diverse AML cell lines (Figure 8) and gene expression analyses (Figure 9).

claim: Peptidomimetic remodeling of oncogenic MYB complexes is accompanied by specific proteolysis of MYB.
source: Peptidomimetic remodeling of oncogenic MYB complexes is accompanied by specific proteolysis and dynamic redistribution of CBP/P300 with alternative transcription factors such as RUNX1 to induce myeloid differentiation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing MYB protein depletion upon CRYBMIM treatment (Figure 10) and rescue by proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: Peptidomimetic remodeling of oncogenic MYB complexes causes dynamic redistribution of CBP/P300 with alternative transcription factors such as RUNX1.
source: Peptidomimetic remodeling of oncogenic MYB complexes is accompanied by specific proteolysis and dynamic redistribution of CBP/P300 with alternative transcription factors such as RUNX1 to induce myeloid differentiation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing CBP/P300 redistribution (Figure 6) and co-immunoprecipitation showing increased RUNX1:CBP/P300 binding upon CRYBMIM treatment (Figure 12).

claim: Aberrant assembly and sequestration of MYB:CBP/P300 complexes provide a unifying mechanism of oncogenic gene expression in AML.
source: Thus, aberrant assembly and sequestration of MYB:CBP/P300 complexes provide a unifying mechanism of oncogenic gene expression in AML.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective experimental data showing convergent MYB complex organization across diverse AML subtypes and CBP/P300 redistribution upon peptidomimetic treatment.

claim: Gene dysregulation is one of the most prevalent features in human cancers (Bradner et al., 2017).
source: Gene dysregulation is one of the most prevalent features in human cancers (Bradner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aberrant gene expression contributes to most important properties of leukemia cells, including self-renewal, growth, and resistance to therapy.
source: In blood cancers, and acute myeloid leukemias (AML) in particular, aberrant gene expression is thought to contribute to most important properties of leukemia cells, including self-renewal, growth, and resistance to therapy.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Numerous pathogenic chromosomal translocations in AML, such as those involving AML1 (RUNX1) and MLL1 (KMT2A) produce chimeric transcription or chromatin remodeling factors that cause disease (Look, 1997).
source: For example, numerous pathogenic chromosomal translocations in AML, such as those involving AML1 (RUNX1) and MLL1 (KMT2A) produce chimeric transcription or chromatin remodeling factors that cause disease (Look, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DOT1L or Menin inhibition is effective for MLL-rearranged leukemias (Krivtsov et al., 2019).
source: While specific molecular dependencies have been identified for some genetic subtypes of AML, such as DOT1L or Menin inhibition for MLL-rearranged leukemias (Krivtsov et al., 2019), and CARM1 inhibition for AML1-rearranged leukemias (Greenblatt et al., 2019), distinct pathogenetic mechanisms of diverse AML subtypes also appear to converge on shared molecular pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CARM1 inhibition is effective for AML1-rearranged leukemias (Greenblatt et al., 2019).
source: While specific molecular dependencies have been identified for some genetic subtypes of AML, such as DOT1L or Menin inhibition for MLL-rearranged leukemias (Krivtsov et al., 2019), and CARM1 inhibition for AML1-rearranged leukemias (Greenblatt et al., 2019), distinct pathogenetic mechanisms of diverse AML subtypes also appear to converge on shared molecular pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 25% of adult and childhood AMLs, including both MLL-rearranged and non-rearranged cases, require aberrant activation of the transcription factor MEF2C (Brown et al., 2018; Tarumoto et al., 2018; Vakoc and Kentsis, 2018).
source: For example, approximately 25% of adult and childhood AMLs, including both MLL-rearranged and non-rearranged cases, require aberrant activation of the transcription factor MEF2C, conferring susceptibility to MARK and SIK inhibitors, which are currently being explored for clinical trials for patients (Brown et al., 2018; Tarumoto et al., 2018; Vakoc and Kentsis, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nearly 50% of examined AML specimens exhibit aberrant activation of HGF/MET/FGFR signaling (Kentsis et al., 2012).
source: Similarly, nearly 50% of examined AML specimens exhibit aberrant activation of HGF/MET/FGFR signaling (Kentsis et al., 2012) and are being currently targeted therapeutically in the ongoing clinical trial of combined MET and FGFR inhibitors in patients with relapsed or refractory AML (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT03125239).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Transient suppression of Myb nearly completely eliminates leukemia development in mouse models in vivo while sparing normal hematopoietic cells (Zuber et al., 2011).
source: Recently, MYB has emerged as a therapeutic target in AML, as transient suppression of Myb nearly completely eliminates leukemia development in mouse models in vivo while sparing normal hematopoietic cells (Zuber et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pioneering studies have implicated Myb as a key mediator of leukemias (Klempnauer and Bishop, 1984; Luger et al., 2002).
source: Indeed, pioneering studies have implicated Myb as a key mediator of leukemias (Klempnauer and Bishop, 1984; Luger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MYB is the cellular homologue of the viral v-Myb oncogene that can cause avian leukemias and function as a pioneer transcription factor in mammalian cells (Biedenkapp et al., 1988).
source: MYB is the cellular homologue of the viral v-Myb oncogene that can cause avian leukemias and function as a pioneer transcription factor in mammalian cells (Biedenkapp et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MYB functions as a master regulator of gene expression in diverse cell types, including hematopoietic cells where it controls cell proliferation and differentiation (Ramsay and Gonda, 2008).
source: MYB functions as a master regulator of gene expression in diverse cell types, including hematopoietic cells where it controls cell proliferation and differentiation (Ramsay and Gonda, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aberrant expression of TAL1 in T-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (T-ALL) is induced by pathogenic somatic mutations that create neomorphic MYB-binding sites (Mansour et al., 2014).
source: For example, aberrant expression of TAL1 in T-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (T-ALL) is induced by pathogenic somatic mutations that create neomorphic MYB-binding sites (Mansour et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MYB is recurrently rearranged in distinct subtype of blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasms (BPDCN) (Suzuki et al., 2017).
source: Likewise, MYB is recurrently rearranged in distinct subtype of blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasms (BPDCN), a highly refractory hematologic malignancy (Suzuki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Booreana strain of mice that impairs the binding of Myb by its co-activator CBP/P300 (Crebbp/Ep300) due to the mutation of Myb E308G is resistant to leukemogenesis induced by MLL-AF9 and AML1-ETO oncogenes but has largely normal hematopoiesis (Pattabiraman et al., 2014).
source: Notably, the Booreana strain of mice that impairs the binding of Myb by its co-activator CBP/P300 (Crebbp/Ep300) due to the mutation of Myb E308G in its transcriptional activation domain is resistant to leukemogenesis induced by the otherwise fully penetrant MLL-AF9 and AML1-ETO oncogenes but has largely normal hematopoiesis (Pattabiraman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A peptidomimetic inhibitor of MYB:CBP/P300 was previously developed (Ramaswamy et al., 2018).
source: Recently, we developed a peptidomimetic inhibitor of MYB:CBP/P300 (Ramaswamy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: CBP depletion was the most significantly required gene to confer resistance to MYBMIM in a genome-wide CRISPR screen.
source: The most significantly affected gene whose depletion was required to confer resistance to MYBMIM was CBP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the genome-wide CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CBP depletion exhibited no enrichment upon PBS treatment in the CRISPR screen.
source: In contrast, CBP depletion exhibited no enrichment upon PBS treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MYBMIM is a specific inhibitor of MYB:CBP.
source: Thus, MYBMIM is a specific inhibitor of MYB:CBP, and emphasizes the exquisite specificity of peptidomimetic inhibitors as pharmacologic modulators of protein interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CRISPR screen results showing CBP as the top hit for resistance.

claim: MYB is the most significantly required human gene in 37 leukemia cell lines, including 20 AML cell lines, of diverse molecular subtypes (p=1.1e-15).
source: We found that MYB is the most significantly required human gene in 37 leukemia cell lines, including 20 AML cell lines, of diverse molecular subtypes (p=1.1e-15; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DepMap Cancer Dependency Map data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MYB target gene activation requires its specific interaction with CREB-binding protein (CBP)/P300 for co-activation (Dai et al., 1996).
source: MYB target gene activation requires its specific interaction with CREB-binding protein (CBP)/P300 for co-activation (Dai et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The helical MYB transactivation domain comprising residues 293–310 binds to the KIX domain of CBP/P300 (Zor et al., 2004).
source: The helical MYB transactivation domain comprising residues 293–310 binds to the KIX domain of CBP/P300 (Zor et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MYBMIM bound to recombinant CBP KIX domain with the dissociation constant of 21.3 ± 2.9 µM, as compared to the native MYB peptide of 4.2 ± 0.5 µM (Ramaswamy et al., 2018).
source: Given that MYBMIM bound to recombinant CBP KIX domain with the dissociation constant of 21.3 ± 2.9 µM, as compared to the native MYB peptide of 4.2 ± 0.5 µM (Ramaswamy et al., 2018), we reasoned that a peptidomimetic inhibitor with higher affinity to CBP/P300 would be more effective.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: CRYBMIM binds to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with Kd of 5.7 ± 0.2 µM.
source: As expected, both CRYBMIM and CREBMIM bind to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with significantly improved (three-- to six-fold) affinities as compared to MYBMIM and measured by microscale thermophoresis (Kd of 5.7 ± 0.2 µM, 2.9 ± 0.7 µM, and 17.3 ± 1.6 µM, p=1e-15; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CREBMIM binds to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with Kd of 2.9 ± 0.7 µM.
source: As expected, both CRYBMIM and CREBMIM bind to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with significantly improved (three-- to six-fold) affinities as compared to MYBMIM and measured by microscale thermophoresis (Kd of 5.7 ± 0.2 µM, 2.9 ± 0.7 µM, and 17.3 ± 1.6 µM, p=1e-15; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MYBMIM binds to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with Kd of 17.3 ± 1.6 µM.
source: As expected, both CRYBMIM and CREBMIM bind to the purified recombinant CBP KIX domain with significantly improved (three-- to six-fold) affinities as compared to MYBMIM and measured by microscale thermophoresis (Kd of 5.7 ± 0.2 µM, 2.9 ± 0.7 µM, and 17.3 ± 1.6 µM, p=1e-15; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CRYBMIM can compete with the binding of CBP/P300 to immobilized CRYBMIM with apparent Ki of approximately 4.7 µM.
source: We found that increasing concentrations of free CRYBMIM could compete with the binding of CBP/P300 to immobilized CRYBMIM, with the apparent Ki of approximately 4.7 µM based on quantitative fluorescence densitometry measurements (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by competition binding assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CREBMIM is significantly less effective at displacing CBP/P300 from immobilized CREBMIM (apparent Ki >100 µM).
source: In contrast, excess CREBMIM was significantly less effective at displacing CBP/P300 from immobilized CREBMIM (apparent Ki >100 µM, Figure 2E–F), consistent with the much higher nM affinity and allosteric effects that characterize the CREB:CBP/P300 interaction (Goto et al., 2002; Radhakrishnan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by competition binding assays shown in Figure 2E-F and citations to prior literature on CREB:CBP/P300 interaction.

claim: CRYBMIM binds CBP/P300 specifically, not MED15.
source: Importantly, CRYBMIM binds CBP/P300 specifically, as exposure of AML cell extracts to streptavidin-immobilized biotinylated CRYBMIM leads to efficient binding to CBP/P300, but not MED15 which is highly expressed in MV411 AML cells and contains a known KIX domain with the closest sequence similarity to CBP/P300 (38% identity; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FITC-CRYBMIM and FITC-CREBMIM efficiently localized to the nuclei of MV411 AML cells within 1 hr of peptide treatment.
source: Consistently, we observed that both FITC-CRYBMIM and FITC-CREBMIM efficiently localized to the nuclei of MV411 AML cells within 1 hr of peptide treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment induced substantial depletion of MYB from the immunoprecipitated CBP/P300 complex at 10 μM for 1 hr.
source: Under these more stringent conditions, we found that CRYBMIM is indeed more potent compared to MYBMIM, as evidenced by the substantial depletion of MYB from the immunoprecipitated CBP/P300 complex by CRYBMIM but not MYBMIM under these conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither CREBMIM nor CRYBMIM treatment interfered with the binding of CREB to the cellular CBP/P300 complex.
source: Neither CREBMIM nor CRYBMIM treatment interfered with the binding of CREB to the cellular CBP/P300 complex (Figure 3B), in agreement with the affinities of their direct binding to the recombinant CBP KIX domain (Figure 2D–F), the nM affinity of CREB:CBP/P300 interaction (Radhakrishnan et al., 1997), and the specific molecular features required for MYB but not CREB or MLL1 binding (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior literature.

claim: CRYBMIM exhibited significantly higher potency against MV411 AML cells compared to MYBMIM, CREBMIM and MLLMIM (IC50 = 6.9 ± 3.4 µM, 13 ± 3.3, 29 ± 3.8 µM, and 24 ± 2.0 µM, p=1e-15).
source: Consistent with this prediction, we observed that CRYBMIM exhibited significantly higher potency against MV411 AML cells, as compared to MYBMIM as well as CREBMIM and MLLMIM (IC50 = 6.9 ± 3.4 µM, 13 ± 3.3, 29 ± 3.8 µM, and 24 ± 2.0 µM, p=1e-15; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The inactive analogue CG3 exhibited significantly reduced activity compared to CRYBMIM (IC50 of 17 ± 1.0 µM, p=2.75e-4).
source: We confirmed CRYBMIM's specificity by analyzing its inactive analogue CG3 and MYBMIM's inactive analogue TG3, in which three residues forming key electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with the KIX domain were replaced by glycines; both exhibited significantly reduced activity (IC50 of 17 ± 1.0 µM and 49 ± 2.6 µM, p=2.75e-4 and <1e-15, respectively; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The inactive analogue TG3 exhibited significantly reduced activity compared to MYBMIM (IC50 of 49 ± 2.6 µM, p<1e-15).
source: We confirmed CRYBMIM's specificity by analyzing its inactive analogue CG3 and MYBMIM's inactive analogue TG3, in which three residues forming key electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with the KIX domain were replaced by glycines; both exhibited significantly reduced activity (IC50 of 17 ± 1.0 µM and 49 ± 2.6 µM, p=2.75e-4 and <1e-15, respectively; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CRYBMIM had minimal effects on the clonogenic growth of normal CD34+ progenitor cells compared to MV411 AML cells (91 ± 3.8% versus 47 ± 2.4% colonies, p=1e-4).
source: We observed minimal effects on the clonogenic growth of normal progenitor cells, as compared to that of MV411 AML cells which was significantly suppressed (91 ± 3.8% versus 47 ± 2.4% colonies, p=1e-4; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by colony forming assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CRYBMIM achieved more than 1000-fold suppression of MV411 cell growth after 6 days of treatment compared to control (p=8.6e-3).
source: For example, whereas MYBMIM induced nearly 100-fold suppression of growth of MV411 cells after 6 days of treatment in agreement with prior studies (Ramaswamy et al., 2018), CRYBMIM achieved more than 1000-fold suppression compared to control (p=8.6e-3; Figure 3G), consistent with its improved biochemical affinity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 3G and comparison to prior work.

claim: CRYBMIM had broad-spectrum activity against diverse AML subtypes (10 of 11 cell lines tested).
source: This improved activity of CRYBMIM spanned diverse AML subtypes, including MLL-rearranged, AML1-ETO translocated, PML-RARA-translocated, DNMT3A-mutant, NPM1c-mutant, TP53-mutant, MYC-amplified, and WT1-mutant cell lines, with the exception of erythroblastic BCR-ABL1-translocated K562 cells (10 of 11 cell lines tested; Figure 3G and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Depletion of CBP caused significant resistance to CRYBMIM in MOLM13 cells (p=6.0e-10 and 4.0e-8 for sgCBP-1 and sgCBP-2).
source: In contrast, depletion of CBP had no significant effects on steady-state cell fitness, but caused significant resistance to CRYBMIM, where CBP-deficient cells outcompeted their non-transduced counterparts when treated with CRYBMIM (p=6.0e-10 and 4.0e-8 for sgCBP-1 and sgCBP-2 in MOLM13 cells, respectively, and 1.1e-6 and 3.7e-6 for MV411 cells; Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR competitive assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of CBP caused significant resistance to CRYBMIM in MV411 cells (p=1.1e-6 and 3.7e-6 for sgCBP-1 and sgCBP-2).
source: In contrast, depletion of CBP had no significant effects on steady-state cell fitness, but caused significant resistance to CRYBMIM, where CBP-deficient cells outcompeted their non-transduced counterparts when treated with CRYBMIM (p=6.0e-10 and 4.0e-8 for sgCBP-1 and sgCBP-2 in MOLM13 cells, respectively, and 1.1e-6 and 3.7e-6 for MV411 cells; Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR competitive assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CBP and EP300 contribute to distinct gene expression programs required for susceptibility to peptidomimetic blockade.
source: This suggests that CBP and EP300 contribute to distinct gene expression programs, presumably as part of specific transcription factor complexes, as required for their susceptibility to peptidomimetic blockade.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of CBP versus EP300 depletion on CRYBMIM susceptibility.

claim: After 4-hr duration of CRYBMIM treatment, 2869 genes were significantly downregulated, including known MYB target genes MYC, IKZF1, GATA2, and KIT.
source: We found that after 4-hr duration of treatment, CRYBMIM causes significant downregulation of 2869 genes, including known MYB target genes MYC, IKZF1, GATA2, and KIT (Figure 5A–C, Supplementary file 2b-e).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: CRYBMIM caused significant upregulation of 4099 genes after 4 hr of treatment.
source: Similar to MYBMIM, CRYBMIM also caused significant upregulation of distinct genes, an effect that was substantially more pronounced upon 4 hr of treatment (4099 genes; 5A-B, Supplementary file 2b-e).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed significant induction of myeloid and monocyte differentiation programs upon CRYBMIM treatment.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the expected suppression of MYB target genes (Figure 5C), gene set enrichment analysis also revealed significant induction of myeloid and monocyte differentiation programs (Figure 5D–E and Supplementary file 2f).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: CRYBMIM induced significant increases in the AP-1 family transcription factors FOS and JUN, as well as IL6 and CSF1.
source: For example, CRYBMIM induced significant increases in the AP-1 family transcription factors FOS and JUN, as well as IL6 and CSF1 that control myeloid differentiation (Figure 5B; Gonda et al., 1993; Selvakumaran et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B and citations to prior literature on myeloid differentiation.

claim: Nearly 40% of the genes induced by deletion of RUVBL2 were also found to be induced by CRYBMIM treatment, including JUN, FOS, and FOSB (Armenteros-Monterroso et al., 2019).
source: Nearly 40% of the genes induced by deletion of RUVBL2 were also found to be induced by CRYBMIM treatment, including JUN, FOS, and FOSB (Armenteros-Monterroso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to prior literature on RUVBL2 deletion effects.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment induced significant phenotypic differentiation of MV411 cells, as evidenced by the induction of monocytic CD11b expression.
source: In agreement with these findings, CRYBMIM treatment induced significant phenotypic differentiation of MV411 cells, as evidenced by the induction of monocytic CD11b expression, as measured by flow cytometry (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment leads to significant redistribution of both MYB and CBP/P300 on chromatin.
source: Consistently, we found that CRYBMIM treatment leads to significant redistribution of both MYB and CBP/P300 on chromatin (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: After 4 hours of CRYBMIM treatment, MYB was significantly depleted from 2587 promoters and enhancers.
source: By 4 hours of CRYBMIM treatment, MYB was significantly depleted from 2587 promoters and enhancers, primarily at sites associated with the MYB DNA-binding motifs, as well as motifs corresponding to NFY, ETS family, AP-1 family, SP1, and C/EBP family member transcription factors (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: CBP/P300 was depleted from 7579 genes and redistributed to 11,324 new loci after 4 hours of CRYBMIM treatment.
source: Noticeably, CBP/P300 was not only depleted from 7579 genes, but also significantly redistributed to 11,324 new loci (Figure 6D), consistent with the remodeling of its complex upon CRYBMIM treatment.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Loci that gained CBP/P300 upon CRYBMIM treatment were enriched in DNA-binding motifs for the AP-1, RUNX1, EGR, and C/EBP family member transcription factors.
source: Likewise, loci that gained CBP/P300 upon CRYBMIM treatment were enriched in DNA-binding motifs for the AP-1, RUNX1, EGR, and C/EBP family member transcription factors (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 724 unique proteins are specifically associated with MYB in MV411 AML cells.
source: To control for abundant proteins and other contaminants that may co-purify non-specifically, we used non-specific isotype control antibodies and precursor ion quantitation to establish stringent statistical parameters that led to the identification of 724 unique proteins that are specifically associated with MYB in MV411 AML cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by affinity purification-mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CBP was identified in the MYB complex by high-confidence identification of unique peptide spectra that distinguish CBP from P300.
source: This included CBP itself, as confirmed by the high-confidence identification of unique peptide spectra that distinguish CBP from P300, with four additional peptides shared by both CBP and P300 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as well as other known MYB interactors such as CEBPB (Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry peptide identification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 59 chromatin-associated proteins are functionally non-redundant MYB:CBP co-factors.
source: We found that these genes encode factors with diverse molecular functions, including a group of 59 chromatin-associated proteins (Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: This is supported by integration of mass spectrometry and CRISPR dependency data.

claim: 10 MYB-associated factors were selectively required for 37 leukemia but not 615 other non-hematopoietic cancer cells lines.
source: Indeed, 10 such factors were selectively required for 37 leukemia but not 615 other non-hematopoietic cancer cells lines (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DepMap dependency data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In all seven AML cell lines tested, MYB was physically associated with LYL1 and E2A transcription factors.
source: We found that in all seven cell lines tested, MYB was physically associated with LYL1 and E2A transcription factors (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LMO2 was physically associated with MYB in all cell lines except OCIAML2.
source: In contrast, LMO2 was physically associated with MYB in all cell lines except OCIAML2, CEBPA was co-assembled with MYB in OCIAML2 and U937 cells, and SATB1 was co-assembled with MYB in MV411 and HL60 cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CEBPA was co-assembled with MYB in OCIAML2 and U937 cells.
source: In contrast, LMO2 was physically associated with MYB in all cell lines except OCIAML2, CEBPA was co-assembled with MYB in OCIAML2 and U937 cells, and SATB1 was co-assembled with MYB in MV411 and HL60 cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: SATB1 was co-assembled with MYB in MV411 and HL60 cells.
source: In contrast, LMO2 was physically associated with MYB in all cell lines except OCIAML2, CEBPA was co-assembled with MYB in OCIAML2 and U937 cells, and SATB1 was co-assembled with MYB in MV411 and HL60 cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CEBPA and SATB1 were measurably expressed exclusively in AML cells among the blood cell types examined.
source: We found that most transcription factors that are assembled with MYB in diverse AML cell lines could be detected in one or more normal human blood cells, albeit with variable abundance, with the exception of CEBPA and SATB1 that were measurably expressed exclusively in AML cells (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Principal component analysis exhibited excellent separation between CRYBMIM-sensitive and less sensitive cell lines, with PC1 (62%) and PC2 (19%) explaining more than 80% of the variability in CRYBMIM susceptibility.
source: We found that this approach exhibited excellent separation between CRYBMIM-sensitive (MV411, OCIAML2, OCIAML3, HL60) and less sensitive (Kasumi1, K562) cell lines, with the first (PC1, 62%) and second (PC2, 19%) eigenvectors explaining more than 80% of the variability in CRYBMIM susceptibility (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The protein abundance levels of CEBPA and LYL1 exhibited the greatest contribution to the observed clustering of CRYBMIM susceptibility.
source: In particular, the protein abundance levels of CEBPA and LYL1 exhibited the greatest contribution to the observed clustering (Figure 9C), consistent with their observed activity in MYB-assembled chromatin dynamics (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: MYB and CBP/P300 complexes were highly enriched in LYL1, SATB1, E2A, and LMO2 in MV411 and HL60 AML cells but not in normal umbilical cord blood mononuclear cells.
source: While MYB, CBP/P300 and LYL1 were physically associated in normal umbilical cord blood mononuclear cells, we did not observe their physical association with E2A, SATB1 and LMO2. In contrast, MYB and CBP/P300 complexes were highly enriched in LYL1, SATB1, E2A, and LMO2 in MV411 and HL60 AML cells (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: A shared set of genes was suppressed in expression upon CRYBMIM treatment of all AML cell lines tested, such as MYC.
source: In agreement with the prediction, we observed a shared set of genes that was suppressed in expression upon CRYBMIM treatment of all AML cell lines, such as MYC for example (Figure 5A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: A shared set of genes was induced by CRYBMIM treatment across AML cell lines, including genes associated with hematopoietic differentiation such as FOS, JUN, and ATF3.
source: Similarly, we observed a shared set of genes that was induced by CRYBMIM treatment, including numerous genes associated with hematopoietic differentiation such as FOS, JUN, and ATF3, as well as SERPINE, KLF6, DDIT3, and NFKBIZ (Figure 5A–B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment induced nearly 10-fold reductions in cellular MYB protein levels with exponential kinetics on the time-scale of 1–4 hr in CRYBMIM-sensitive MV411, HL60, OCIAML2, and OCIAML3 cells.
source: We found that CRYBMIM treatment induced nearly 10-fold reductions in cellular MYB protein levels with exponential kinetics on the time-scale of 1–4 hr in CRYBMIM-sensitive MV411, HL60, OCIAML2, and OCIAML3 cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Susceptibility of diverse AML cell lines to CRYBMIM was significantly correlated with the apparent kinetics of MYB protein decay (Pearson r = 0.94).
source: Susceptibility of diverse AML cell lines to CRYBMIM, as measured by cell viability (Figure 3G), was significantly correlated with the apparent kinetics of MYB protein decay (Pearson r = 0.94; Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: MG132 co-treatment led to near complete rescue of CRYBMIM-induced MYB protein depletion.
source: Consistent with the proteolytic depletion of MYB upon CRYBMIM treatment, MG132 co-treatment led to near complete rescue of this effect (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Overexpression of BCL2 was unable to rescue CRYBMIM-induced proteolysis of MYB.
source: This effect was specific because overexpression of BCL2, which blocks MYBMIM-induced apoptosis (Ramaswamy et al., 2018), and rescued the depletion of cellular CREB, presumably due to non-specific proteolysis that accompanies apoptosis, was unable to rescue CRYBMIM-induced proteolysis of MYB (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 10C and citation to prior work.

claim: Approximately one-third of the affected genes lost both MYB and CBP/P300 in response to CRYBMIM, as well as RUNX1, LYL1, and/or CEBPA.
source: Approximately one-third of the affected genes lost both MYB and CBP/P300 in response to CRYBMIM, as well as RUNX1, LYL1, and/or CEBPA (Figure 11B; yellow clusters 1, 3, and 6).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Genes in the MYB and CBP/P300-depleted clusters 1, 3, and 6 were enriched in those associated with the development of hematopoietic progenitor cells, as well as MYC and HOXA9/MEIS1 targets.
source: Genes in the MYB and CBP/P300-depleted clusters 1, 3, and 6 were enriched in those associated with the development of hematopoietic progenitor cells, as well as MYC and HOXA9/MEIS1 targets (Supplementary file 3c), consistent with current and past gene expression profiling studies (Figure 5 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq clusters.

claim: The two chromatin dynamics clusters 4 and 9 that gained both MYB and CBP/P300 in response to CRYBMIM were enriched in genes controlling myeloid differentiation programs.
source: Notably, the two chromatin dynamics clusters 4 and 9 that gained both MYB and CBP/P300 in response to CRYBMIM, associated with the accumulation of CEBPA, RUNX1, and/or CREB, were enriched in genes controlling myeloid differentiation programs (Figure 11B; orange, and Supplementary file 3c).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq clustering and gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 11B.

claim: CRYBMIM-induced accumulation of CBP/P300 at the FOS locus was associated with increased binding of RUNX1, and eviction of CEBPA and LYL1.
source: In the case of FOS, we observed that CRYBMIM-induced accumulation of CBP/P300 was associated with increased binding of RUNX1, and eviction of CEBPA and LYL1 (Figure 11—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Assembly of RUNX1 with CBP/P300 was increased by more than fourfold upon CRYBMIM treatment (p=3.4e-4).
source: In contrast, whereas no detectable RUNX1 was found co-associated with MYB either at baseline or upon CRYBMIM treatment (Figure 12A), assembly of RUNX1 with CBP/P300 was increased by more than fourfold upon CRYBMIM treatment, as measured by image densitometry (p=3.4e-4; Figure 12B–C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and quantification data shown in Figure 12B-C.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment caused substantial depletion of CBP/P300 from immunoprecipitated MYB complexes.
source: In agreement with biochemical studies, we observed substantial depletion of CBP/P300 from immunoprecipitated MYB complexes upon CRYBMIM treatment (Figure 12A), and of MYB from immunoprecipitated CBP/300 complexes (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 12A-B.

claim: CRYBMIM treatment caused reduced binding of LYL1, SATB1, E2A, LMO2, and CEBPA to MYB and CBP/P300 complexes.
source: Similarly, we observed reduced binding of LYL1, SATB1, E2A, LMO2, and CEBPA.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 12A-B.
